Title: Anorexia Nervosa Register-based Severity Trajectories: Polygenic and Comorbid Associations
Authors: Abdulkadir, M.; Larsen, J. T.; Zhang, Z.-P.; Musliner, K. L.; Clausen, L.; Bulik, C.; Petersen, L. V.; Yilmaz, Z.
Abstract: ImportanceAnorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe psychiatric disorder with heterogeneous outcomes and elevated mortality. Characterizing severity trajectories may improve early risk stratification and targeted intervention.  ObjectiveTo identify AN severity trajectories using a register-based severity index (AN-RSI) and examine their associations with polygenic scores (PGS), preceding (prior to AN diagnosis) as well as subsequent (beyond 5 years post AN diagnosis) psychiatric and somatic disorders.  DesignPopulation-based cohort study.  SettingNationwide study in Denmark.  ParticipantsIndividuals born between 1963 and 2007 with diagnosed AN (N = 9534 individuals). Genetic data were available in a subsample (N = 5126).  ExposuresForty-one PGS indexing traits relevant to AN, and psychiatric and somatic disorders prior to AN diagnosis.  Main Outcomes and MeasuresAN-RSI trajectories, psychiatric, and somatic disorders beyond 5 years post AN diagnosis.  ResultsThree trajectories were identified: "low and stable" (32.6%), "medium and stable" (53.5%), and "high increasing" (14.0%). The "low and stable" group was used as the comparison group for all analyses. Each 1 standard deviation (SD) increase in AN PGS corresponded with 13% greater odds of following the "high increasing" trajectory. Increases in BMI and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) PGS corresponded with 15% and 14% lower odds of following the "high increasing" trajectory, respectively. No preceding psychiatric or somatic disorders were significantly associated with trajectory membership. In contrast, subsequent psychiatric and somatic disorders were more likely in individuals following the "high increasing" trajectory with odds ratios ranging between 1.7 (ADHD) and 3.7 (psychoactive substance dependence) for psychiatric disorders and between 1.6 (poor fetal growth of child) and 4 (microcytic anemia) for somatic disorders.  Conclusions and RelevanceOur findings demonstrate that individuals with AN follow distinct severity trajectories that are associated with differences in polygenic risk and post-diagnostic morbidity patterns but not with pre-diagnosis psychiatric or somatic morbidity. As the field progresses, incorporating PGS into comprehensive assessments at first presentation may aid in early identification, personalized intervention, and resource allocation for individuals at higher risk of developing a severe illness trajectory.  Key pointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSDo patients with anorexia nervosa follow distinct severity trajectories that are associated with specific genetic and morbidity risks?  FindingsIn this register-based study we identified three severity trajectories of anorexia nervosa. Those who followed the most severe illness trajectory had greater genetic liability to lower body weight and anorexia nervosa and were at greater risk for developing subsequent psychiatric and somatic disorders.  MeaningIllness severity trajectories in anorexia nervosa marked by genetic risk may assist in early identification and intervention for those at greatest risk of severe illness.

Title: Impact of DENV-ZIKV cross-reactivity in Southeast Asia: A modelling study in Thailand
Authors: Shi, Y.; Senapati, A.; Huang, A. T.; Clapham, H. E.
Abstract: Dengue virus (DENV) is endemic across Southeast Asia (SEA), where a large proportion of adults have been infected. Zika virus (ZIKV) has circulated in the region for decades but the extent of transmission remains unclear. Prior infection with one virus can protect against or enhance infection with the other, but the population-level consequences are unknown. We developed an age-structured DENV-ZIKV model with nine cross-reactivity assumptions combining cross-protection and subsequent enhancement, and simulated sustained co-circulation under changing Thai demography. Through cross-reactivity, DENV strongly shaped ZIKV transmission, whereas ZIKV had little effect on DENV transmission. Under cross-protection, ZIKV transmission occurred as infrequent outbreaks without changes in long-term ZIKV burden. When prior DENV infection enhanced both ZIKV infection and symptomatic risk, this burden roughly doubled. Population ageing raised the mean age of DENV and ZIKV cases by over 20 years, more than cross-reactivity did. Simulated ZIKV case ages were closer to those reported in Thailand in 2019-2023 under enhancement of ZIKV infection and symptoms. Over half of individuals aged 15-49 years remained ZIKV-naive under all assumptions, leaving many pregnancies at risk of congenital Zika syndrome. Interpreting ZIKV case counts in SEA requires joint consideration of cross-reactivity, demographic change and case detection.

Title: Exploring the Barriers and Facilitators of Vaccine Procurement in Health Districts of the South West Region of Cameroon
Authors: Theophile, F. B.; Fru-Cho, J.; Fankam, N. F.; Tabi, E. S. B.; Yoah, T. A.; Akoachere, J.-F. T. K.
Abstract: BackgroundImmunization is the most cost-effective way of preventing vaccine-preventable diseases and reducing morbidity and mortality in children 0 to 5 years old. The vaccine procurement capacity of health districts significantly influences the vaccine coverage rates. The advent of the socio-political crisis in the North West and South West Regions of Cameroon could have had a negative bearing on vaccine procurement and thus coverage rates. Thus, this study was carried out to explore the barriers and facilitators of vaccine procurement in health districts of a South West Region of Cameroon. This will help reduce vaccine stock-out at the health district level and increase vaccine coverage.  MethodologyA qualitative study was conducted using in-depth interviews (IDIs) to collect data from healthcare providers in all the 21 health districts in the South West Region working with the Expanded Program on Immunization (EPI), and who met the inclusion criteria. A Delphi consensus approach was employed to formulate feasible facilitators to the optimization of vaccine procurement. Data was analysed using Nvivo 11. Thematic analysis was used to explore the barriers to vaccine procurement at the level of health districts. A Delphi consensus of [≥] 70.0% was considered acceptable.  ResultsFrom the thematic analysis, nine broad themes: financial constraints, limited workforce, inadequate transportation logistics, poor equipment, inadequate managerial skills, inadequate in-service training, vaccine stock-out and weak primary health care (PHC) system facilities emerged as barriers to vaccine procurement. Of the 12 strategies retained for the optimization of vaccine procurement, 5 (41.7%) were priority strategies: provision of extra solar refrigerators (100.0%), WHO certification training for EPI staff (100.0%), financial allocation for transport (100.0%), equipment and training, in-service training for both district and health facility staff (100.0%), resolving the socio-political crisis (100.0%) and provision of specialized transport logistics for maritime Health Districts (100.0%).  ConclusionFinancing of vaccine procurement, recruitment/certification of staff, provision of transportation logistics, provision of solar refrigerators, regular supervision, organization of in-service training, with focus on requisition/stock and bulk-requisition were the main strategies suggested to overcome the barriers to vaccine procurement.  RecommendationsThese findings highlight the need for all stakeholders to co-finance and manage vaccine procurement at the health district level in the South West Region of Cameroon.

Title: Wealth inequalities malaria parasitaemia and child anaemia in Nigeria
Authors: Fowobaje, K. R.; Adegbenro, A.; Lawson, T.
Abstract: Anaemia and malaria remain concentrated among children living in poorer households in Nigeria, but the extent to which the wealth gradient in anaemia operates through current malaria parasitaemia is uncertain. We used three nationally representative surveys to estimate a clearly defined parasitaemia-mediated component of the association, while recognising that anaemia has multiple infectious, nutritional, genetic, and social causes.  We analysed de facto children aged 6-59 months in the 2010, 2015, and 2021 Nigeria Malaria Indicator Surveys. Within each survey, we contrasted children in the poorest quintile with children in the richer and richest quintiles. The outcome was altitude-adjusted anaemia and the mediator was microscopy-confirmed parasitaemia. Weighted outcome and mediator models adjusted for child age and sex, maternal education, urban residence, geopolitical zone, household size, rainy-season interview, and altitude. We standardized interventional total, direct, and indirect effects using g- computation. Missing data were addressed with 20 chained-equation imputations; uncertainty used 1,000 Rao-Wu survey-bootstrap replicates.  Analytic samples included 3,307, 3,643, and 6,572 children in 2010, 2015, and 2021. The multiple-imputation total risk difference was 11.0 (95% CI 4.1 to 17.9) percentage points in 2015 and 12.5 (95% CI 8.4 to 16.6) points in 2021; corresponding parasitaemia-mediated indirect differences were 3.4 (95% CI 1.4 to 5.4) and 2.0 (95% CI 1.1 to 2.9) points. The 2010 total-effect interval included zero. Proportion-mediated estimates were withheld for 2010 and 2015 because of unstable total- effect denominators.  The poorest-to-richer/richest contrast was associated with higher anaemia risk in 2015 and 2021. A smaller positive component was compatible with mediation through microscopy-confirmed parasitaemia. Because wealth, parasitaemia, and haemoglobin were measured in the same survey visit, the estimates require assumptions about temporal ordering and unmeasured mediator-outcome confounding; they do not establish that eliminating parasitaemia would remove the observed anaemia inequality.

Title: Implementing community-based minimally invasive tissue sampling for mortality surveillance in rural South Africa: A process evaluation of the Vukamberi project
Authors: Mondlane, Z. L.; Kahn, K.; Chipungu, S.; Wagner, R. G.; Tippett Barr, B.; Price, J.
Abstract: Accurate cause-of-death data are limited in rural low- and middle-income settings, where most deaths occur at home without medical certification. Minimally invasive tissue sampling (MITS) is a culturally acceptable alternative to complete autopsy but has largely been applied to stillbirths and child deaths. We evaluated the process and implementation of a community-based, all-age MITS study in rural South Africa.  The Vukamberi project ("to examine" in Xitsonga) is a prospective study in rural Bushbuckridge sub-district, Mpumalanga Province. Guided by the Medical Research Council Framework for Complex Interventions and Proctors Implementation Outcomes Framework, we assessed reach, adoption, fidelity, feasibility, acceptability and timeliness using prospectively collected records of deaths notified between 07 July 2024 to 30 June 2026, and mapped challenges to adaptive strategies by domain and phase.  All 408 notified community deaths were screened, and 316 (77.5%) were eligible. Families consented for 206 eligible cases (65.2%), all of which proceeded to MITS, with target-organ sampling adherence in 199 (96.6%). Median time from death to notification was 15 hours (interquartile range [IQR] 5-23) and to MITS completion 37 hours (IQR 25-49). Enrolled decedents were 197 adults (95.6%) and 9 paediatric cases (4.4%). Main ineligibility reasons were in-hospital death (excluded by design; 27 cases) and notification beyond 48 hours (26 cases). Family refusal, mostly reflecting grief-related unreadiness and sociocultural barriers, accounted for 53 (48.2%) non-enrolled eligible cases. Adaptive strategies that increased enrolment included extending recruitment beyond the Agincourt Health and Socio- Demographic Surveillance System into the wider sub-district, incentivised community informants, elder-mediated consent, gender-appropriate field staff, non-disfigurement messaging in local languages and mortuary-based consenting where household access was restricted by a traditional leader.  Community-based MITS was feasible in this rural setting. Culturally responsive consent strategies, mortuary partnerships and multi-channel death notification helped overcome sociocultural and logistical barriers, and a reliable supply of consumables proved essential for continuous enrolment. These findings may inform community-based mortality surveillance in other low- and middle-income settings.

Title: Indirect effects of doxyPEP implementation reveal core-group dynamics of bacterial sexually-transmitted infections
Authors: Yechezkel, M.; Kapadia, B.; Hong, V.; Lim, J. T.; Reyes, I. A. C.; Pomichowski, M. E.; Davis, G. S.; Rodriguez Barraquer, I.; Mueller, N. F.; Tartof, S. Y.; Lewnard, J. A.
Abstract: Epidemiological theory holds that core groups of high-risk individuals sustain pathogen transmission. However, the scale at which these dynamics operate is poorly understood. We leveraged doxycycline post-exposure prophylaxis (doxyPEP) implementation among at-risk men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender women (TGW) as a natural experiment to probe bacterial sexually transmitted infection (STI) dynamics within and across sexual networks. DoxyPEP uptake by 9% of at-risk MSM and TGW was associated with pronounced indirect protection within their sexual networks, substantiating the notion that core groups of individuals wield outsize influence on transmission. Risk of chlamydia and syphilis declined by 80% (95% confidence interval: 71-86%) and 65% (30-82%), respectively, among doxyPEP recipients, and by 41% (32-48%) and 29% (13-42%), respectively, among MSM and TGW who did not receive doxyPEP. However, this substantial reduction in disease among at-risk MSM and TGW did not impact incidence among females and other males. Our findings substantiate core group dynamics of STIs among MSM and TGW but call into question the "bisexual bridge" hypothesis positioning this population as a core group impacting STI dynamics among heterosexuals. These findings should inform rational expectations for the impacts of doxyPEP in settings implementing this intervention.

Title: Mapping inequalities in dementia diagnosis in England: a Bayesian spatial analysis of disease prevalence and case ascertainment
Authors: Taylor, B.; Jiang, J.; Warren, J. D.; Crutch, S. J.
Abstract: BackgroundBy 2030, over one million people in the UK are projected to be living with dementia; however, the NHS estimates that only approximately 65% of individuals with dementia currently receive a formal diagnosis. Understanding the geographic and socioeconomic factors contributing to variation in diagnosis is essential for reducing inequalities in dementia care.  MethodsWe developed a Bayesian spatial modelling framework to separate underlying dementia prevalence from case ascertainment using routinely collected public datasets at Local Authority District (LAD) level across England. Underlying prevalence was modelled using non-modifiable and modifiable risk factors identified by the Lancet Commission, while diagnosis rates were modelled as a function of healthcare provision and sociodemographic factors. Spatial random effects were incorporated to identify residual geographic variation after accounting for observed covariates. We additionally compared case ascertainment with regional variation in dementia subtype coding as a further measure of diagnostic quality.  FindingsSubstantial geographic variation in dementia diagnosis remained after accounting for differences in underlying disease prevalence. Urbanicity, deprivation, ethnicity, and healthcare provision were associated with variation in case ascertainment, with spatial effects explaining additional regional variation. Diagnostic specificity varied considerably between regions, with areas of lower case ascertainment tending to exhibit higher proportions of undifferentiated dementia diagnoses.  InterpretationBy jointly modelling underlying dementia prevalence and case ascertainment, we can distinguish the factors associated with dementia burden from those associated with diagnosis. This enables the identification of areas with low case ascertainment, which when combined with poor diagnostic specificity, provides an evidence base for targeted regional interventions. Potential interventions include strengthening dementia care pathways through enhanced outreach, more equitable access to diagnostic assessment, and locally tailored models of care.

Title: Impact of transnational gentrification on the health of adults from the EPIPorto cohort: a quasi-experimental study
Authors: Figueiredo, J. A.; Alves, H.; Moreira, C.; Ribeiro, A. I.
Abstract: Gentrification is a global, accelerating urban process involving complex socio-spatial transformations. Although increasingly recognised as a determinant of urban health, quantitative evidence on its population health impacts remains scarce and inconsistent, limiting evidence-informed urban policymaking, especially in rapidly gentrifying contexts. Thus, we assessed the health impact of neighbourhood-level gentrification among adults in Porto (Northern Portugal), a hotspot of transnational gentrification. A quasi-experimental study was conducted using data from the EPIPorto population-based cohort (1999-2022), with 2,485 participants at baseline. A validated, context-sensitive 16-variable index of transnational gentrification, derived from 2011 and 2021 census and tourism-accommodation data through Principal Component Analysis, enabled neighbourhood classification as gentrifying or non-gentrifying. Difference-in-differences models estimated the effect of living in gentrifying neighbourhoods on ten cardiometabolic and behavioural outcomes. Inverse probability of censoring weighting was used to account for loss to follow-up and missing data. At baseline, 26.2% of participants resided in gentrifying neighbourhoods. Residence in a gentrifying neighbourhood was associated with a statistically significant reduction in nightly sleep duration (-0.346 h; 95% CI -0.650, -0.042), with statistically significant reductions in the lower-education and [≥]65-year subgroups. No significant effects were observed for body mass index, overweight/obesity, total/HDL/LDL cholesterol, blood pressure, and tobacco or alcohol use. Transnational gentrification in Porto showed limited effects on most cardiometabolic outcomes but was associated with reduced sleep duration, suggesting that the health impacts of gentrification may initially emerge through psychosocial pathways before translating into measurable cardiometabolic changes.

Title: Dengue among febrile patients in Ghana: prevalence and facility-level variation in a multisite surveillance study
Authors: Zigah, F.; Agyei-Nkansah, A. A.; Tagoe, E. A.; Gyapon, I. A. T.; Bonney, K.; Adomako-Boateng, F.; Punguyire, D. T.; Oliver-Commey, J. A.; Adzesi, R. S.; Sagoe, K. W. C.; Afrane, Y. A.; Pappoe-Ashong, P. J. P.-A. J.; Kenu, E.; Grobbee, D. E.; van der Sande, M. A. B.
Abstract: IntroductionDengue is under-recognized in Ghana, where laboratory testing is limited. We estimated dengue NS1 and/or IgM positivity among febrile patients and described geographical, temporal, and demographic variation.  MethodologyWe conducted cross-sectional surveillance among consenting febrile patients aged [≥]1 year at six public facilities in Greater Accra, Bono East, and Upper West between August 2023 and July 2025. We randomly selected one region within each of three ecological strata and selected facilities with high febrile-case volumes. We approached and recruited consecutive eligible patients. We tested serum for dengue NS1 antigen and IgM antibody by ELISA; positive NS1 samples underwent RT-PCR and serotyping. We estimated proportions with 95% confidence intervals (CI) and used logistic regression to examine adjusted associations.  ResultsAmong 2,936 participants, 204 were NS1- and/or IgM-positive (6.95%; 95% CI, 6.05-7.93%): 31 were NS1-only, 161 IgM-only, and 12 dual-positive. Prevalence ranged from 3.88% (95% CI, 2.19-6.31%) at Kintampo to 12.32% (9.56-15.55%) at Atebubu, both in Bono East. Adjusted odds increased with age (aOR per five years, 1.09; 95% CI, 1.05-1.14). Eight of 43 NS1-positive samples contained dengue RNA: five DENV-1 from Bono East and three DENV-3 from Upper West. There was no clear rainy-dry season difference.  ConclusionsDengue NS1 and/or IgM were detected among febrile patients at all six facilities, and RT-PCR confirmed circulation of DENV-1 and DENV-3. These findings support including dengue in febrile illness evaluation and strengthening laboratory-supported surveillance in Ghana.  Author summaryDengue is probably overlooked in Ghana because its symptoms resemble malaria and other common causes of fever, while laboratory testing is not routinely available. We studied 2,936 febrile patients who attended six public health facilities across three regions of Ghana. Blood samples were tested for a dengue protein found early in infection and for antibodies that usually appear later. Overall, 204 participants (6.95%; 95% confidence interval, 6.05-7.93%) had evidence of acute or recent dengue infection. Dengue was detected at every participating facility, but proportions varied considerably, even among facilities in the same region. Genetic testing detected dengue virus in eight samples and identified virus types 1 and 3. The chance of a positive result increased with age, although this difference was mainly related to antibody detection rather than the early-infection protein. We did not find a simple difference between rainy and dry seasons. Because the facilities were selected for their high numbers of patients with fever, the findings do not estimate dengue prevalence in the general population or across entire regions. They show that dengue contributes to febrile illness in Ghana and support continued surveillance that reports findings separately for individual facilities and diagnostic markers.

Title: Reconstructing age-specific social contact patterns across 28 EU/EEA countries during the COVID-19 pandemic: linking non-pharmaceutical interventions to social mixing, 2020-2022
Authors: Chatzilena, A.; Brooks-Pollock, E.; Colman, E.; Hansson, D.; Demiris, N.; Franklin, B.; Danon, L.
Abstract: In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, most EU/EEA countries sequentially introduced non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) to reduce social contacts and mitigate transmission. The CoMix study captured real-time changes in social mixing, but substantial spatiotemporal gaps remain, with some countries lacking pandemic contact data. We developed a model-based framework to estimate time-varying changes in age-specific contact patterns and relate these changes to NPIs recorded in the ECDC-JRC Response Measures Database. This relationship was used to predict contacts during periods without CoMix observations. For countries without CoMix data, we reconstructed temporal age-specific mixing patterns using estimates from countries with pandemic contact data selected through a country-matching process based on socio-demographic characteristics and similarity in NPI implementation. We generated age-specific contact matrices for 28 EU/EEA countries spanning 2020-2022. Reconstructed patterns captured substantial temporal and cross-country variation in social mixing and its evolving association with NPIs across diverse European contexts. Our framework provides estimates that extend incomplete pandemic contact data across both time and countries, yielding a consistent set of age-specific contact matrices for the EU/EEA. These estimates address important gaps in empirical social-contact data and provide valuable insights into the interplay of NPIs and social mixing patterns which is of critical importance to improving epidemic modelling and policy making.

Title: Effect of starting metformin on severe and long COVID-19 among people living with type 2 diabetes in England: a new user cohort study in OpenSAFELY-TPP
Authors: Amstutz, A.; Walker, V.; Madley-Dowd, P.; Denholm, R.; Zou, M.; Palmer, T. M.; OpenSAFELY Collaborative,  ; Eastwood, S. V.; Hulme, W. J.; Sterne, J. A. C.
Abstract: IntroductionObservational studies report lower COVID-19 mortality among metformin users, but most used prevalent-user designs comparing long-term survivors with heterogeneous controls. Randomised trials suggest little or no mortality effect. No large observational study has used a new-user design to estimate the effect of starting versus not starting metformin on severe and Long COVID outcomes in adults with type 2 diabetes (T2D). We aimed to estimate this effect on COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death, COVID-19 diagnoses, and Long COVID among adults with T2D in England.  Research design and methodsUsing OpenSAFELY-TPP linked NHS electronic health records, we conducted a population-based cohort study with a landmark new-user design. Adults aged 18-85 years newly diagnosed with T2D (August 2018-August 2019) were classified as starting metformin monotherapy within 6 months or not starting any antidiabetic drug, based on prescription data. Follow-up began 6 months after diagnosis and before the UK pandemic (avoiding immortal time) for up to 2 years. We estimated intention-to-treat and per-protocol effects using weighted Cox and pooled logistic regression, with negative (bone fracture) and positive (diabetes-related death) control outcomes.  ResultsOf 52,341 eligible people, 19,599 (37.4%) started metformin. For COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death, the maximally adjusted hazard ratio (HR) of metformin versus no antidiabetic was 1.17 (95% CI 1.02-1.35; 2-year risk difference 0.36%, 95% CI 0.09-0.62; intention-to-treat). The per-protocol HR for COVID-19-related hospitalisation or death was 1.11 (95% CI 0.96-1.29). The Long COVID estimate was imprecise (HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.83-2.33; intention-to-treat). For bone fracture (negative control) the estimate was null (HR 1.00), but for diabetes-related deaths (positive control) it was elevated (HR 1.41, 95% CI 1.09-1.81), indicating unmeasured confounding.  ConclusionsThe risks of severe and long COVID were slightly higher among people who started metformin, compared with those who did not start. These results plausibly reflect unmeasured confounding. These findings align more closely with randomised evidence than earlier prevalent-user studies and argue against a clinically meaningful benefit of starting metformin for COVID-19 prevention in newly diagnosed T2D.  What is already known on this topicObservational studies and their meta-analyses have consistently reported 30-40% lower COVID-19 mortality among metformin users, yet most used prevalent-user designs that compare long-term survivors with mixed control groups and can overstate benefit. Randomised trials suggest little or no effect on mortality.  What this study addsUsing a new-user design in more than 52,000 adults with newly diagnosed T2D, risks of severe and long COVID were slightly higher among people who started metformin, compared with those who did not start. These results plausibly reflect unmeasured confounding rather than harm.  How this study might affect research, practice or policyThese findings align with randomised evidence and argue against a clinically meaningful benefit of starting metformin for preventing severe or Long COVID in people with T2D. They also illustrate how new-user designs can reconcile discrepant observational and trial results and should be prioritised in future drug-repurposing studies.  Lay summaryMetformin is a medication commonly used to treat type 2 diabetes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, some studies suggested it might also protect against severe COVID-19, but many such studies had design limitations that could have made metformin look more beneficial than it truly is. In this study, we used NHS health records from over 52,000 adults in England who were newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes to examine whether starting metformin shortly after diagnosis reduced the risk of being hospitalised or dying from COVID-19, being diagnosed with COVID-19. We found no evidence that starting metformin protected against any of these outcomes, although the effect on long COVID was imprecisely estimated. Our findings are consistent with results from clinical trials and suggest that metformin should not be expected to prevent severe COVID-19 in people with type 2 diabetes.

Title: Lipidome-wide analysis of concurrent and longitudinal blood pressure patterns in school-aged children
Authors: ALFANO, R.; nawrot, t.; barth, k.; giesberts, n.; renaers, e.; vangeneugden, m.; Plusquin, M.
Abstract: BackgroundElevated blood pressure (BP) in childhood is associated with cardiovascular risk, but its molecular lipid correlates remain poorly characterized. We investigated the association of plasma lipid species and patterns with concurrent and longitudinal BP phenotypes in school-aged children.  MethodsIn the Belgian ENVIRONAGE prospective birth-cohort, 195 children aged 9 to 12 years were examined between July 2021 and September 2024. A total of 1,232 plasma lipid species were quantified using liquid chromatography-electrospray ionization-tandem mass spectrometry. Associations with systolic and diastolic BP percentiles were examined using multivariable linear regression with permutation-based family-wise error rate (FWER) correction. Lipid-set enrichment analysis, with P values from sample permutation to account for correlation among lipid species, evaluated coordinated associations. Significant findings were examined across longitudinal BP patterns in 177 children with BP measured at ages 4-6 and 9-12.  FindingsEach 1-SD increase in triglyceride (TG) 58:9 fatty acyl (FA) 22:4 was associated with 7.36 higher systolic BP percentile points (95% CI=3.91-10.80; PFWER=0.03). TG 58:9 FA 22:4 was associated with incident (OR=2.78; 95% CI=1.33-5.79) and persistent (OR=2.14; 95% CI=1.22-3.77), but not resolved elevated BP vs stable-normal BP. Among lipid sets, species with a total carbon number of 38, mainly PC and PE, were inversely enriched with diastolic BP percentile.  InterpretationChildhood BP was associated with higher levels of a highly polyunsaturated long-chain TG, closely related to current BP elevation and not elevated among children whose BP had normalized.  FundingSpecial Research Fund, Flemish Scientific Research Fund, Methusalem and Kom op Tegen Kanker.  Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed for studies published from inception to 13 October 2026, without language restrictions, for human studies, using the following combinations of terms: ("child*" OR "adolescen*") AND ("blood pressure" OR "hypertension") AND ("lipidomic*" OR "lipidome"). Previous pediatric studies have implicated glycerophospholipids, sphingolipids and triglycerides, but most were conducted in specific clinical, dietary, environmental, or ethnic settings. We found little population-based evidence from comprehensive lipidome-wide analyses and no studies examining whether lipidomic signatures differ according to longitudinal blood pressure patterns spanning early and later childhood.  Added value of this studyIn a population-based birth cohort, we measured 1,232 lipid species in plasma from 195 children aged 9-12 years and related them to blood pressure at that age and at ages 4-6 years. One long-chain, highly unsaturated triglyceride was associated with higher systolic blood pressure. The triglyceride association was present in children whose blood pressure became or remained elevated, but not in those whose elevated blood pressure had normalized. Accounting for the correlation among lipids, only one lipid group, phospholipids with 38 carbon atoms, was inversely enriched with diastolic blood pressure.  Implications of all the available evidenceTogether with adult studies linking triglyceride species to hypertension, our findings suggest that a triglyceride species is also associated with blood pressure in children. The lead triglyceride species was more closely related to current elevation, and was not detectable in children with normal current blood pressure but earlier elevation. Smaller signatures of earlier blood pressure cannot be excluded, studies with repeated lipidomics and blood pressure assessment from early childhood are needed to determine whether earlier blood pressure leaves a more subtle trace in the lipidome.

Title: A dollar-aware food-environment index and a 27-year trajectory typology: a measurement foundation for diet and childhood-obesity research in Mississippi, 1997-2024
Authors: Mandalapu, S. V.; Lefebvre, S.; Walker, E. D.
Abstract: BackgroundThe retail food environment is a widely used exposure in behavioural-nutrition and obesity research. Grocery stores have declined across rural America while limited-assortment discount ("dollar") stores have proliferated, yet standard food-environment indices typically exclude dollar stores. We developed a dollar-aware index, assessed how counting dollar stores changes the measured exposure, and derived a trajectory typology.  MethodsUsing annual establishment data from Data Axle for all 878 Mississippi census tracts (1997-2024), we classified food retailers with code-based rules and computed the modified Retail Food Environment Index (mRFEI) in standard and dollar-aware forms. We fitted latent class tra-jectory models suited to the bounded index, tested their stability in seven sensitivity analyses, and related class membership to the Social Vulnerability Index (SVI) and urbanicity with multinomial regression.  ResultsGrocery stores fell from 1,616 to 716 while dollar stores rose from 315 to 1,005, crossing in 2018. The indices ranked tracts almost identically (within-year Spearman [≥] 0.99), but where dollar stores and healthy outlets coexisted, counting dollar stores lowered the index by 4.5 points in 1997 and 9.1 in 2024, and tracts with only dollar-store retail, which the standard index cannot score, rose from 1 to 32. Six trajectory classes emerged: stable adequate (7.8% of tracts), steady decline (15.3%), early collapse (12.9%), late collapse (9.7%), persistently constrained (34.8%) and chronically low (19.6%); only 7.5% of children in classified tracts lived in stable-adequate tracts. Classes were stable across random starts and pandemic-year exclusion; collapse was robust, but its early-late timing split depended on tracts with few retailers. Chronically low and persistently-constrained tracts were predominantly urban (relative risk ratios 8.3 and 4.5), consistent with food swamps; persistently-constrained and steady-decline membership rose modestly with vulnerability (1.17 and 1.20 per 0.1 SVI), an association that was weaker with 2010 SVI; collapse classes had no cross-sectional social signature.  ConclusionsCounting dollar stores changes the level of a widely used food-environment index, and whether a growing set of tracts can be scored, rather than how tracts rank. A 27-year typology separates urban food swamps from tracts whose food environments collapsed and provides a time-varying exposure for diet and childhood-obesity research.  Contributions to the literatureO_LIStandard food-environment indices omit dollar stores; counting them barely changes how tracts rank, but it lowers index values where dollar stores and healthy outlets coexist and determines whether a growing set of tracts can be scored at all. C_LIO_LIWe provide a 27-year, tract-level trajectory typology of a dollar-aware index, tested in seven sensitivity analyses, that distinguishes urban food swamps from communities whose food environments collapsed. C_LIO_LITracts whose food environments collapsed are indistinguishable from others on present-day social characteristics, illustrating what cross-sectional exposure measures miss. C_LIO_LIWe document data issues that longitudinal food-environment studies using commercial data should check: vendor coverage expansions, store-size fields that shift with vendor coding, and code-based misclassification.
