Title: Serum Raman spectroscopy as a blood-based triage test for bladder cancer: a retrospective proof-of-concept study
Authors: Milligan, K.; Smith, I.; Flugge, A.; Fakhrua Aldeen, N.; Shine, B.; Muldoon, C.
Abstract: BackgroundBladder cancer remains one of the most common urological malignancies. Current diagnostic pathways rely heavily on cystoscopy, an invasive investigation with significant cost and resource implications. A rapid blood-based assay capable of improving patient stratification before cystoscopy could reduce unnecessary invasive investigations while maintaining diagnostic sensitivity.  MethodsArchived serum samples from patients with histologically confirmed bladder cancer and symptomatic control subjects were analysed using dried-serum Raman spectroscopy. Raman spectra were incorporated into supervised machine-learning classification models to generate predicted probabilities of bladder cancer. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis.  ResultsThe study included 49 patients with bladder cancer and 97 symptomatic controls. Predicted probabilities of bladder cancer were substantially higher in cancer patients than in controls. The Raman classifier demonstrated excellent diagnostic discrimination (AUC approximately 0.90). Incorporation of age into the classification model produced little additional improvement (AUC approximately 0.91).  ConclusionsMachine learning-assisted analysis of dried-serum Raman spectra demonstrates promising diagnostic performance for bladder cancer. Prospective evaluation is warranted to determine its role as a minimally invasive triage test within contemporary bladder cancer diagnostic pathways.

Title: Streamlined Point-of-Care Ultrasound Examination for Pulmonary Tuberculosis
Authors: Nakiyingi, L.; Dhamdhere, R.; Nate, W.; Guevarra, K.; Nabawanuka, E.; Jovanovska Janeva, E.; Shankman, R.; Lwanga, E.; Nakabugo, E.; Nasinghe, E.; Nakayenga, S.; Astorga, G.; Sridhar, T. A.; Javvaji, H. K.; Clark, E.; Handler, D.; Salgame, P.; Alland, D.; Joloba, M.; Ellner, J.; Madabhushi, A.; Xie, Y. L.
Abstract: BackgroundPoint-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) is a low-cost, radiation-free triage tool but lacks standardized acquisition protocols for tuberculosis (TB). We developed and evaluated a streamlined symmetric POCUS protocol for pulmonary TB in a high-burden setting.  MethodsUgandan participants aged [≥]13 years with confirmed pulmonary TB, household TB exposure, or a non-TB respiratory condition underwent an 18-position POCUS examination (12 lung zones and 6 pre-established extrapulmonary positions). Random Forest classifiers using prespecified pathologic features were developed in a fixed stratified 75/25 training/holdout split. All symmetric 2-, 4-, and 6-zone combinations were evaluated in training data. The best protocol of each size was locked and tested in the holdout set.  ResultsAmong 318 analyzed participants, 118 (37.1%) had pulmonary TB and 200 were TB-negative, including 102 with other respiratory conditions (ORC). The model-selected 6-zone protocol comprised bilateral anterior-superior, lateral-superior, and posterior-superior lung zones. For TB versus all TB-negative participants, the AUCs for the 6-zone, 12-zone, and 18-position protocols were 0.82 (95% CI, 0.73-0.92), 0.81 (0.70-0.92), and 0.81 (0.71-0.91), respectively (all P > 0.76). For TB versus ORC, AUCs were 0.81 (0.70-0.91), 0.85 (0.76-0.93), and 0.85 (0.76-0.94), respectively (all P > 0.45). The 2-zone protocol had a lower AUC than the 6-zone protocol for TB versus all TB-negative participants (P = 0.004). Shred sign, consolidation, and B-lines with irregular pleura were the strongest TB-associated findings.  ConclusionsA fixed 6-zone lung POCUS examination showed similar discrimination for TB to more comprehensive 12-lung-zone and 18-position protocols. This supports a simpler, scalable approach to TB triage.

Title: Environmental toxic metal exposure and conditional mortality survival among US adults: a prospective cohort study
Authors: Fang, X.; Schwartz, J.
Abstract: Abstract Background. Chronic low-level exposure to lead, cadmium, mercury, and arsenic remains a determinant of premature mortality in the U.S. general population, but previous hazard-ratio analyses do not characterize how exposure shifts the lower tail of the survival distribution, where premature mortality is concentrated. Objectives. We estimated the association of whole-blood lead, whole-blood total mercury, urinary cadmium, and the sum of urinary inorganic and methylated arsenic species with the 10th, 25th, and 50th conditional quantiles of follow-up time to all-cause mortality among U.S. adults aged 40 years and older. Methods. NHANES Continuous 1999 to 2018 was linked to the National Death Index through December 31, 2019 (n = 29,652). Censored quantile regression was fit per metal on the log2 scale at quantiles {tau}{0.10, 0.25, 0.50}. A restricted-cubic-spline (RCS) censored-quantile-regression was fit for blood lead and urinary cadmium to investigate the threshold effect. Results. Over a median follow-up of 9.1 years, 7,215 deaths were ascertained. A doubling of urinary cadmium was associated with -1.57 years of follow-up (95% CI: -2.08, -1.07) at the 10th conditional quantile, -1.50 (-2.04, -0.96) at the 25th, and -1.49 (-1.93, -1.04) at the median (Benjamini Hochberg q < 0.001 throughout). A doubling of whole-blood lead was associated with -0.70 years (95% CI: -0.99, -0.40) at the 10th conditional quantile, -0.62 (-0.92,-0.31) at the 25th, and -0.61 years (-0.89, -0.34) at the median; the absolute loss was largest at {tau} = 0.10 for both metals. Urinary arsenic-metabolite sum was not associated with conditional follow-up at the estimable quantiles. Despite adjustment for dark and fatty-fish intake or DHA/EPA, whole-blood total mercury was associated with longer follow-up (i.e., negatively associated with mortality risk), possibly due to residual confounding by broader dietary or socioeconomic factors, rather than a true protective effect. The cadmium association was additionally robust to the mutual adjustment of lead. Discussion. Low-to-moderate urinary cadmium and whole-blood lead were associated with fewer years of follow-up survival at the lower-tail and median conditional quantiles of survival, with the largest absolute losses at the lower tail of the conditional survival distribution, where premature mortality is concentrated. These findings support continued reductions in U.S. cadmium exposure and lead with particular benefit for adults most vulnerable to premature death.

Title: Associations of drinking water per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances with cause-specific mortality in men with prostate cancer
Authors: Iyer, H. S.; Shanahan, M.; Joseph, S. A.; Varga, J.; He, M. Z.; Ghodoussipour, S.; Stroup, A. M.; Harris, G.; Georgopoulos, P.; Laumbach, R.; Vieira, V.; Hart, J. E.; Barrett, E. S.; Bandera, E. V.
Abstract: Background: Over 3.5 million US men are living with prostate cancer (PCa). Certain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are carcinogenic and impair cardiometabolic health. Due to comorbidities and treatment, men with PCa may be uniquely susceptible to PFAS. Objectives: To develop and validate a model for drinking water perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS), and perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA), and study associations of each PFAS with all-cause, PCa, and cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality in PCa survivors. Methods: We conducted a cohort study of 51,289 men with PCa diagnosed from 2006 to 2017 and followed through 2024 from the New Jersey (NJ) cancer registry. PFAS monitoring data (n=26,161 results) were obtained from NJ government evaluations and Community Water Systems (CWS) compliance reports and were used to estimate PFAS concentrations using a two-phase XGBoost model with 67 predictors of PFAS contamination across 566 CWS. PFAS predictions between 2006-2024 were linked to participant address histories. Adjusted hazard ratios (aHR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) were estimated from Cox models with sociodemographic, clinical and time-varying neighborhood covariates. Results: There were 19,749 deaths, including 3,778 PCa deaths, and 4,972 CVD deaths over 466,843 person-years. Higher PFOA exposure was associated with all-cause mortality in certain quintiles (aHRQ2vsQ1: 1.07, 95% CI: 1.07-1.12; aHRQ3vsQ1: 1.06, 95% CI: 1.01-1.11) and with CVD mortality (aHRQ5vsQ1: 1.12, 95% CI: 1.01-1.24). Higher PFNA exposure was suggestively associated with all-cause mortality (aHR[≥]3.8ng/L vs <2ng/L: 1.22, 95% CI: 0.98-1.50) and PCa mortality (aHR[≥]3.8ng/L vs <2ng/L: 1.42, 95% CI: 0.96-2.10). Associations were strengthened when applying five-year lags. For example, higher PFOA (aHRQ5vsQ1: 1.15, 95% CI: 1.06-1.25), PFOS (aHRQ5vsQ1: 1.16, 95% CI: 1.07-1.25) and PFNA (aHR[≥]3.8ng/L vs <2ng/L: 1.57, 95% CI: 1.06-2.31) were associated with higher all-cause mortality. Discussion: Exposure to CWS-level PFAS was associated with higher mortality in PCa survivors. Replication is needed to confirm findings.

Title: Influenza Vaccination and Disease Severity Among Older Adults Hospitalized with Influenza in France: A Nationwide Cohort Study, 2016-2024
Authors: Abou Chakra, C. N.; Diallo, A. B.; Some, A.; Pitel, B.; Bricout, H.; EL GUERCHE-SEBLAIN, C.; Chauvel, C.; Nunes, M.
Abstract: Objective Seasonal influenza remains a major cause of severe morbidity and mortality among older adults, despite vaccine availability. We assessed whether influenza vaccination was associated with reduced disease severity among adults aged 65 years or more hospitalized with influenza in France. Methods and Analysis We conducted a nationwide retrospective cohort study using the French National Health Data System (SNDS). Adults aged 65 years or more hospitalized with confirmed influenza (ICD-10 codes: J09 or J10) between October 2016 and December 2024 were included, excluding 2020-2021. Vaccination status was identified from reimbursed community pharmacy dispensing records. Entropy balancing was used to balance sociodemographic characteristics, chronic conditions pneumococcal vaccination, and COVID-19 vaccination. Weighted regression models estimated adjusted risk ratios (aRRs) for invasive mechanical ventilation (IMV), intensive care unit (ICU) admission, in-hospital death, and a composite severe outcome. Multistate survival models assessed transitions specific hazard ratios (HR) between hospitalization, ICU, discharge, and in-hospital death. Results Among 132,443 influenza-associated hospitalizations, 72,852 (55%) occurred among vaccinated patients and 59,591 (45%) among unvaccinated patients. Vaccinated patients were older (mean age, 82.3 vs 79.3 years). IMV occurred in 2128 vaccinated (2.9%) and 2544 unvaccinated (4.3%) hospitalizations (aRR, 0.88; 95%CI: 0.83 to 0.93). In-hospital death occurred in 6300 (8.6%) and 4952 (8.3%), respectively (aRR, 0.90; 95%CI: 0.87 to 0.93). Vaccination was also associated with a lower risk of the composite outcome (aRR, 0.96; 95%CI: 0.94 to 0.98), but not ICU admission (aRR, 0.99; 95%CI: 0.96 to 1.01). Among patients admitted to ICU, vaccination was associated with a lower hazard of death (adjusted hazard ratio, 0.85; 95%CI: 0.78 to 0.92) and a 2-day reduction in the median time to discharge. Conclusion In this nationwide cohort study, influenza vaccination was associated with lower risks of IMV and in-hospital death among older adults hospitalized with influenza. These findings are consistent with possible attenuation of disease severity and support efforts to improve influenza vaccination among older adults.

Title: Determinants of mpox vaccine acceptance among peri-urban residents in Sekondi-Takoradi, Western Region of Ghana: A community-based cross-sectional study
Authors: Amugi, G.; Baah, E. M.; Yankey, H.; Kwarkye, I.; Mensah, P.; Jean Claude, K.; Jubin, D.; Kaba Akoriyea, S.; Bekoe, F. A.; Laryea, D.; Abdul-Tawab, A.; Arthur, J.; Kutsoati, S.; Oliver-Commey, J.; Mohammed, N. T.
Abstract: Mpox re-emerged as a global public health concern in 2022, and the Western Region of Ghana became the epicentre of the countrys largest recorded outbreak in 2025. Ahead of a sub-national vaccination campaign launched in October 2025, no study had examined the determinants of mpox vaccine acceptance among peri-urban residents of the region using a theoretically grounded framework. This study determined the sociodemographic and Health Belief Model-based determinants of mpox vaccine acceptance among peri-urban residents of the Sekondi-Takoradi Metropolis, Western Region, Ghana. A community-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 580 adults in six purposively selected peri-urban areas and their surrounding communities between July and August 2025, before the vaccination campaign began. Vaccine acceptance was measured as a three-category outcome (accept, hesitant, refuse) and analysed using chi square tests and multinomial logistic regression adjusted for sociodemographic characteristics, Health Belief Model constructs, and peri-urban area. Overall, 75.7% of respondents were willing to accept the vaccine, 12.9% were hesitant and 11.4% would refuse. Perceived vaccine safety was the strongest determinant: respondents who considered the vaccine very safe had markedly lower adjusted odds of hesitancy (adjusted odds ratio 0.02, 95% confidence interval 0.00-0.12) and refusal (0.03, 0.01-0.13) than those who considered it unsafe. Uncertainty about vaccine effectiveness was associated with hesitancy (9.83, 1.95-49.50), and belief in its effectiveness with lower odds of refusal (0.22, 0.06-0.86). Higher educational attainment was associated with lower odds of hesitancy, being a student or employed with lower odds of refusal, and acceptance differed be 1 tween peri-urban areas (55.1% to 95.6%). Knowledge of mpox transmission was associated with acceptance in bivariate analysis (p < 0.001) but not after adjustment. Risk communication that addresses vaccine safety and effectiveness, rather than generic disease-awareness messaging alone, is likely to be most effec tive in improving mpox vaccine acceptance in this population, with unemployed and less-educated residents warranting targeting. As a pre-campaign baseline collected during an active outbreak, these findings can inform the vaccination response in the Western Region and preparedness in comparable peri-urban West African settings.

Title: An agent-based model of Epstein-Barr virus transmission and vaccination
Authors: Amoako, B.; Huang, Z.; Thommes, E. W.; Hare, W.; Cojocaru, M. G.
Abstract: Epstein- Barr virus (EBV) infects over 90\% of adults worldwide, causing infectious mononucleosis (IM) in adolescents and young adults and contributing to multiple malignancies. Despite its global burden, population- level transmission modeling of EBV remains limited. We present the first population- level agent-based model (ABM) of EBV transmission. The model is implemented with 10,000 agents and calibrated to age-specific seroprevalence data from the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey. Two complementary calibration methods are evaluated, each with its own distinct advantages: Approximate Bayesian Computation (ABC) and Bayesian Optimization with Expected Quantile Improvement (BO- EQI). ABC directly yields an approximate distribution of transmission parameters for propagation through vaccination scenarios. BO- EQI uses a limited simulation budget to identify well-fitting parameter vectors, particularly as the number of fitted parameters increases. We estimate parameter uncertainty at each resolution in a separate Gaussian-kernel posterior analysis, which requires additional simulations and an explicit model for discrepancies between simulated and observed prevalence. As an illustrative application, we simulate the population-level effect of hypothetical EBV vaccines over a 100-year projection horizon. Similar to a previous modeling study, our results suggest that vaccine durability is at least as critical as efficacy, and that a vaccine with direct protection against only EBV may persistently shift IM burden to older ages, an effect our longer simulation horizon reveals to be a durable equilibrium shift rather than a transient cohort phenomenon. These findings highlight the importance of careful vaccine target product profile design; in particular, our results suggest that dual efficacy against both EBV infection and IM progression represents the most promising achievable target profile, and should be a core design objective for next-generation EBV vaccines.

Title: A multi-region discrete time chain binomial model for infectious disease transmission
Authors: Sinha, P. K.; Mukhopadhyay, S.
Abstract: Conventional mathematical models of infectious diseases often overlook the spatial spread of the disease, focusing only on local transmission. However, spatial propagation of various diseases has been observed mainly due to the movement of infectious individuals from one region to another. In this work, we propose a multiregion discrete-time chain binomial framework to model dependencies between infection time series from neighboring regions. The proposed model is based on the epidemiological principle that new infections arise from interactions between susceptible and previously infected individuals. To strengthen the statistical formulation, the probability of new infections within each spatial unit is modeled through a link function, by allowing it to depend on lagged local incidence, inter-regional transmission effects, and region-specific covariates. The framework also allows for higher-order temporal dependence through an AR(p) specification. To reduce complexity of the model as the number of regions increases, sparsity is imposed by using spatial contiguity matrices and k-nearest-neighbor structures. For estimating these multiregion models, an appropriate likelihood function maximization approach is proposed. A predictive likelihood based method is used to generate forecasts of disease counts in connected spatial units. In-depth analyses of two real measles datasets and simulation studies incorporating seasonal patterns, different weight matrices across connected regions, and varying intervention strategies are used to motivate the proposed modeling framework and demonstrate its ability to reproduce realistic outbreak dynamics. While the simulation studies demonstrate applicability of the general AR(p) approach, the real data analysis of measles shows that an AR(1) model is adequate to capture the temporal dependence.

Title: Associations between different intensities of leisure-time physical activity and subsequent psychotropic medication use among young and early midlife adults: a register-linked follow-up study
Authors: Jarvensivu, L.; Paivarinne, V.; Rahkonen, O.; Lallukka, T.
Abstract: Introduction Previous studies have not examined associations between physical activity intensity and subsequent psychotropic medication use. We examined associations between different leisure-time physical activity (LTPA) intensities and subsequent psychotropic medication purchases. Methods We used Helsinki Health Study questionnaire data collected in 2017 from 19-39-year-old employees of the City of Helsinki, linked to register data on psychotropic medication purchases from 2014 to 2022 (82.5% consented to the register linkage). The analytical sample included 4,160 participants (80.4% women, representing the target population). Weekly hours of light (LPA), moderate (MPA) and vigorous (VPA) LTPA were examined separately. Cox proportional hazards regression with restricted cubic splines was used to examine nonlinear associations with the first psychotropic medication purchase during follow-up, adjusting for prior medication and sociodemographic and health-related covariates. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. Results During the follow-up, 28.1% of participants had at least one psychotropic medication purchase. After adjustment for age and gender, VPA was associated with psychotropic medication purchases (overall p<0.001; nonlinearity p<0.001), whereas MPA and LPA were not. Further adjustments and stratification by prior psychotropic medication purchase status attenuated the VPA association (overall p=0.0041). In this model, for 5 versus 0 hours/week of VPA, the HR was 0.79 (95% CI 0.68-0.91), corresponding to approximately 23 fewer first-purchase events per 1,000 participants over three years. Conclusions Higher-intensity LTPA appeared more strongly associated with a lower hazard of psychotropic medication purchases, although only the VPA association saw clear support.

Title: Diversifying deaths: the shifting spectrum of childhood respiratory infectious mortality, 1990-2023: a systematic analysis of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
Authors: Li, D.; Chen, H.; Wang, X.; Shen, C.
Abstract: Background Childhood respiratory infectious deaths are partitioned across four Global Burden of Disease cause modules-26 etiological attributions within lower respiratory infections, tuberculosis, COVID-19, and whooping cough-never jointly reported. Whether the structure of this combined mortality spectrum has changed over time, and with what implications for intervention design, has not been quantified. We assembled and analyzed the integrated spectrum for children and adolescents aged 0-19 years, 1990-2023. Methods We integrated Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 (release v8352) estimates into a 29-node spectrum-26 lower respiratory infection etiologies plus tuberculosis, COVID-19, and pertussis-globally and across seven super-regions, with uncertainty propagated by summing bounds. We computed Shannon diversity, Herfindahl concentration, and effective cause counts; phenotyped pandemic-window collapse and rebound per cause; linked pathogen shares to WHO/UNICEF vaccine coverage; and mapped geographic concentration in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. Reporting follows GATHER. Segmented (joinpoint) log-linear models with breakpoints selected by the Bayesian information criterion were fitted to annual totals, Shannon diversity and leading pathogen shares. Results In 2023 the 29 causes jointly accounted for 965,330 deaths (95% uncertainty interval [UI] 680,096-1,342,437). Shannon diversity rose from 2.336 to 2.711 (+16.1%) between 1990 and 2023; the effective number of causes nearly doubled (5.57 to 9.94), inversely coupled to total deaths (Spearman rho = -0.997). Whooping cough ranked second (112,954 deaths; 95% UI 64,576-185,708; 11.7%) and showed the spectrum's only rebound above 100% (-57.4% collapse, +111.0% rebound). Tuberculosis ranked third (87,764; 57,779-124,912; 9.1%) with the highest concentration in sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia (87.1%). COVID-19 entered at rank five (52,899; 47,275-59,183; 5.5%). Nineteen of 29 causes exceeded the poverty-lock threshold (>80.59% of deaths in sub-Saharan Africa plus South Asia). Joinpoint analysis placed breakpoints in total deaths at 2011, 2018 and 2021-the decline slowed from -3.4% to -2.3% per year after 2011, steepened to -7.1% per year in 2018-2021 and rebounded +4.5% per year in 2021-2023-while diversification accelerated to +1.18% per year in 2013-2020; all six leading pathogen shares carried a pandemic-window breakpoint at 2019 and 2021 (S. pneumoniae at 2018 and 2021). Conclusions Childhood respiratory infectious mortality has become more diverse and more concentrated in poverty as it has declined. Single-pathogen interventions now address a shrinking share; the spectrum's structure argues for platform interventions-oxygen, antimicrobial access, referral-tailored jointly by age and geography, implying that pathogen-specific strategies alone cannot finish the remaining mortality agenda.

Title: Human Plasma Proteomics Links Modifiable Lifestyle Exposome to Disease Risk
Authors: Isaac, S. K.; Ellis, R. J.; Jee, Y. H.; Murthy, V. L.; Udler, M. S.; Neale, B.; Sunyaev, S.; Gusev, A.; Martin, A.; Patel, C. J.
Abstract: Lifestyle exposures influence disease risk, yet the molecular signatures linking modifiable behaviors to human biology remain incompletely characterized. Here we show that the plasma proteome carries a measurable record of modifiable lifestyle exposures. We developed the Human Exposomic Architecture of the Proteome (HEAP), a framework linking lifestyle exposures, plasma proteins, and disease risk at population scale. Applying HEAP to more than 50,000 UK Biobank participants, 2,686 plasma proteins, and 169 lifestyle exposures, we identified exposure-associated protein signatures that organized along shared health-behavior patterns and connected lifestyle variation to disease-relevant biology. Integrating disease associations, mediation analyses, Mendelian randomization, and colocalization showed that only a minority of exposure-responsive proteins were consistent with causal intermediates, whereas many appeared to function as biological reporters of exposure burden, disease liability, and early disease processes. Comparisons with exercise-training and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist studies linked observational lifestyle signatures to intervention-induced proteomic changes, suggesting that part of the exposomic signal reflects biology modifiable by intervention. Furthermore, proteome-based exposure scores captured exposure-associated biology, tracked behavioral change over time, and predicted disease risk. Overall, HEAP provides a resource for advancing disease prevention and precision medicine by linking modifiable lifestyle exposures to disease-relevant protein signatures.

Title: Geographic prioritization of child nutrition services in Bangladesh: comparing stunting and wasting indicators using the 2025 Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey
Authors: Hoque, S. M. A. U.; Islam, M. K.; Hasan, M. K.; Sharif, M. M.; Naher, T.; Banu, B.; Hossain, Z. Z.; Baset, K. u.
Abstract: Background: Bangladesh's progress on stunting leaves policymakers with a practical question about wasting: where should they focus limited resources? The country met its 2025 stunting target, yet child wasting rose from 9.8% in 2019 to 12.9% in 2025. We assessed whether prioritizing districts with the highest stunting prevalence would include a greater share of children with wasting than proportional allocation at the same child-population coverage. Methods: We used the 2025 Bangladesh Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey to rank all 64 districts by stunting or wasting prevalence. Among 22,311 children under five with valid weight-for-height measurements, we estimated the share of children with wasting who lived in the highest-ranked districts. We compared rankings with population-proportional allocation at 10%, 20%, and 30% child-population coverage, interpolating within the last district to match coverage exactly. We estimated uncertainty using 2,000 paired survey bootstrap replicates and assessed how well district wasting rankings from 2019 carried forward to 2025. Results: At 20% coverage, districts ranked highest for stunting contained 19.5% of children with wasting (95% CI 17.8 to 22.6), a difference of -0.5 percentage points from proportional allocation (95% CI -2.2 to 2.6). Differences were also small at 10% (-0.3 points, 95% CI -1.6 to 1.2) and 30% coverage (1.3 points, 95% CI -2.3 to 3.3). The four stunting hotspot districts contained 5.9% of all children and 5.9% of children with wasting. At 20% coverage, ranking districts by 2025 wasting prevalence captured 26.3% of children with wasting in-sample and 24.3% after correction for optimism. The 2019 wasting ranking captured 22.9% (95% CI 19.0 to 24.2). Conclusions: A stunting map should not guide where Bangladesh prioritizes districts for child wasting. High-stunting districts held wasted children only in proportion to their population. Wasting rankings from 2019 kept an uncertain advantage. Wasting prioritization needs its own, more frequent data.

Title: Kangaroo Mother Care coverage and quality in 66 neonatal units implementing with NEST360 across Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria, and Tanzania
Authors: Reynolds, E.; Thomas, J.; Gicheha, E. W.; Shemwell, K.; Dougherty, K.; Magombo, C. C.; Mochache, D.; Mutakyamilwa, J. C.; Soko, G. T.; Idowu, A. A.; Muinde, D.; Waiyego, M.; Tongo, O.; Salim, N.; Shabani, J.; Ezeaka, V. C.; Macharia, W.; Chiume, M.; Kawaza, K.; Ngwala, S. K.; Okello, G.; Odedere, O.; Paul, C.; Malla, L.; Wainaina, J.; Oden, Z. M.; Richards-Kortum, R.; Hirschhorn, L. R.; Lawn, J. E.; Rhoda, N. R.; Murless-Collins, S.; Bohne, C. A.
Abstract: BackgroundKangaroo Mother Care (KMC) reduces neonatal mortality and morbidity among preterm and low birthweight (LBW) infants, but implementation and quality vary across sub-Saharan African (SSA) hospitals. This study reports KMC coverage and quality of care for preterm and LBW neonates admitted to hospitals in the NEST360 Alliance (Kenya, Malawi, Tanzania, Nigeria) and examines the association between KMC provision and survival to discharge.  MethodsWe conducted a cross-sectional study using routinely collected neonatal inpatient data from hospitals participating in the NEST360 Alliance. Newborns weighing under 2500g were eligible for KMC and included in coverage and quality analyses (January 2021-December 2024). Quality-of-care cascades quantified attrition along the KMC care pathway from eligibility to successful delivery, defining quality as the proportion of eligible neonates reaching each successive step. Mixed-effects logistic regression assessed the association between KMC and survival at discharge, including variation by illness severity and, among KMC recipients, by timing of initiation across severity and birthweight strata.  ResultsOf 375,238 neonatal admissions across 66 hospitals, 125,844 neonates were eligible for KMC and had KMC documentation available. Among these, 64,619 (51.3%) received KMC. All four countries showed improved coverage over the study period, with the largest absolute increases in Nigeria (27.6%) and Tanzania (27.4%). Excluding Kenya, where KMC timing data were unavailable, 92.1% of neonates started on KMC had a documented start date; of these 44,264 neonates, 12,934 (29.2%) were initiated on KMC on the first day of life. The quality cascade showed eligible neonates were lost at each step, from eligibility through to documented, timely, and sustained KMC. Among neonates eligible for both KMC and CPAP, 39.4% of those started on KMC also received documented CPAP at some point during admission. After adjustment for patient-level factors, receiving KMC was associated with improved survival across all severity groups, with the greatest absolute benefit among the most critically ill neonates (adjusted predicted survival 7% vs 80% without and with KMC, respectively).  ConclusionKMC coverage improved substantially across NEST360-implementing hospitals between 2021 and 2024, demonstrating progress in implementation. However, important gaps remain in the quality and timeliness of KMC delivery. More investment in high-quality KMC implementation, supported by robust monitoring systems linked with quality improvement, are essential to improve outcomes for small and sick newborns across sub-Saharan Africa.  KEY FINDINGS1. WHAT WAS KNOWN?O_LIKangaroo Mother Care (KMC) is an evidence-based intervention that reduces mortality in preterm neonates, with updated 2022 WHO guidelines extending eligibility to all infants weighing less than 2500g and recommending initiation as soon as possible after birth. C_LIO_LICoverage of KMC across sub-Saharan Africa remains consistently below global targets, with persistent gaps between policy commitment and delivery at hospital level. C_LIO_LIMonitoring both coverage and quality at scale has been hindered by limited availability of reliable, routinely collected data. C_LI  Key gap to addressO_LILarge-scale, individually-linked data quantifying both KMC coverage and quality across multiple countries and hospitals in sub-Saharan Africa were lacking, and no prior study had applied a quality-of-care cascade framework to systematically identify gaps across the KMC care pathway. C_LI  2. WHAT WAS DONE THAT IS NEW?O_LIThis study analysed prospectively collected, individually-linked neonatal inpatient data from 66 hospitals across four countries (Kenya, Malawi, Nigeria, and Tanzania) implementing with NEST360 between 2021 and 2024, covering 375,238 admissions and 125,844 KMC-eligible neonates. C_LIO_LIA quality-of-care cascade, adapted from the HIV clinical cascade, defines quality by progression through successive steps and quantifies losses among eligible neonates at each step towards timely, documented, and sustained KMC, including co-interventions. C_LIO_LIIndividually linked records allow each neonate to be followed from admission to discharge or death, enabling adjustment for severity and identification of the specific points at which care is lost, a granularity rarely available in routine aggregated data. C_LI  3. WHAT WAS FOUND?O_LIOf 145,513 KMC-eligible neonates, 125,844 (86.5%) had documentation showing whether KMC was administered or not, and KMC coverage increased across all four countries over the study period, with the largest absolute increases in Nigeria (27.6%) and Tanzania (27.4%). C_LIO_LIHowever, after excluding Kenyan facilities because KMC timing data were unavailable during the study period, only 7.5% of eligible neonates received KMC on the first day of life, suggesting that timely initiation of KMC remained limited despite WHO guidance recommending immediate initiation. C_LIO_LIAmong neonates eligible for both KMC and CPAP, 39.4% of those started on KMC also received documented CPAP administration, highlighting limited delivery of both interventions during admission among neonates with the highest clinical need C_LIO_LIAfter adjustment for patient-level factors, KMC was strongly associated with improved survival across all illness severity groups, with the greatest absolute benefit observed among the most critically ill neonates (adjusted predicted survival 7% vs 80% without and with KMC, respectively). The apparent survival advantage associated with later KMC initiation likely reflects survivor selection bias, whereby only clinically stable neonates survived long enough to receive KMC after the first day. C_LI  4. WHAT NEXT?O_LIProgrammes should incorporate KMC initiation time as a standard quality indicator alongside coverage, shifting towards effective coverage frameworks that account for both receipt and the conditions under which care is delivered. C_LIO_LIProgrammes should also ensure that there is continued support for KMC through targeted mentoring, quality improvement as well as investment in supportive infrastructure. C_LIO_LIStrengthening and standardising clinical documentation systems is essential to accurately measure and monitor KMC delivery at scale. C_LIO_LIFuture data collection within NEST360 should incorporate KMC duration as a quality indicator, including through integration into the Neonatal Inpatient Dataset (NID), to capture this critical dimension of KMC effectiveness that the current analysis was unable to assess. C_LIO_LITo improve measurement and action for routine measurement and relevant indicators for KMC. Duration is crucial to test, both for NEST360 and wider use. C_LI

Title: Genomic diversity of respiratory pathogens in clinical versus community surveillance: a comparative analysis of SARS-CoV-2, RSV, and influenza viruses in Washington State
Authors: Kirsch, J. M.; Elias-Warren, A.; Frisbie, L.; Lockwood, C.; Weil, A. A.; Black, A.; Chu, H. Y.; Roychoudhury, P.
Abstract: Background Genomic surveillance of respiratory viruses typically relies on sequences from individuals seeking health care, and whether these sequences represent the viruses circulating in the community is not well-characterized. We aimed to compare the diversity, proportion, and dynamics of influenza, respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), and SARS-CoV-2 between clinical and community samples. Methods In this retrospective comparative genomic analysis, we used whole-genome sequences from community-based surveillance studies in the Seattle area, and clinical sequences from the Washington State Department of Health. We compared clade proportions and dynamics, sequence-cluster diversity, non-synonymous mutations, and Ct values between clinical and community samples. Findings We analyzed 538 RSV sequences collected between 2019 and 2021 (278 community, 260 clinical), 1506 influenza sequences (260 community, 1246 clinical) between 2019 and 2020, and 8660 SARS-CoV-2 sequences (5923 community, 2737 clinical) from 2020 to 2022. Clade proportions did not differ between clinical and community samples for RSV or influenza, but differed for SARS-CoV-2: clades 21J (Delta) and 21K (Omicron BA.1) were more frequent in community samples and clade 22B (Omicron BA.5) in clinical samples. SARS-CoV-2 clinical sequence clusters were more diverse than community clusters, whereas RSV and influenza showed no significant difference. Several spike mutations associated with monoclonal antibody resistance were more prevalent in community samples for SARS-CoV-2. Ct values were lower in clinical samples for multiple SARS-CoV-2, RSV, and influenza clades. Interpretation Seasonal respiratory viruses had similar dynamics and diversity in clinical and community samples, whereas pandemic SARS-CoV-2 differed between settings. Genomic surveillance programs should combine clinical and community sampling, particularly during pandemics in order to better capture viral diversity.

Title: Epidemiology of zero-dose among children aged 12-35 months in Ethiopia: Burden, correlates and spatial patterns; Evidence from a 2025 national survey
Authors: Geleso, M. G.; Shiferie, F.; Worku, A.; Asres, A.; Astatkie, A.; Shumet, T.; Tsegaye, D. A.; Andargie, G.; Gebremedhin, S.
Abstract: Background: Children who have not received the first dose of a diphtheria-tetanus-pertussis-containing vaccine are classified as zero-dose. Understanding how many children remain without this dose beyond infancy, the correlates, and their geographic distribution can inform routine and catch-up vaccination services in Ethiopia. This study aimed to estimate the burden of zero-dose, identify its correlates, and map its spatial distribution among children aged 12-35 months in Ethiopia. Methods: We analyzed data from 2,097 children aged 12-35 months in the Pathways for Ethiopia survey, a recent national population-based cross-sectional household survey conducted from August to November 2025. The burden estimates and regression analyses accounted for sampling weights, stratification, and clustering. Adjusted prevalence ratios (aPRs) were obtained through marginal standardization of survey-weighted logistic regression models. Spatial autocorrelation, hotspot, and spatial-scan analyses assessed geographic clustering. Ordinary kriging predicted prevalence at unsampled locations. Results: The weighted prevalence of zero-dose status was 20.6% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 15.9-26.3), with regional point estimates ranging from 0.8% in Addis Ababa to 35.9% in Somali. Its burden was 20.4% among children aged 12-23 months and 20.8% among those aged 24-35 months. Higher burden was associated with no antenatal care compared with four or more visits (aPR: 2.39; 95% CI: 1.61-3.53), unimproved compared with improved drinking-water sources (aPR: 1.52; 95% CI: 1.18-1.97), and caregivers rating vaccination as less than very important compared with very important (aPR: 2.68; 95% CI: 2.03-3.54). Zero-dose prevalence showed significant spatial clustering (Morans I = 0.229; p = 0.0001). Hotspots occurred among sampled communities in Somali, Oromia, Central Ethiopia, Afar, and South Ethiopia. Predicted prevalence was highest across parts of eastern and south-central Ethiopia. Conclusion: Approximately one in five children aged 12-35 months had not received the first pentavalent dose. High zero-dose prevalence clustered among sampled communities in eastern and south-central Ethiopia. Moreover, antenatal care and drinking water source were independent factors. Immunization programs should prioritize these communities for identifying and vaccinating missed children, including those aged 24-35 months.

Title: Socioeconomic position, socioenvironmental conditions, and subjective cognitive decline among midlife and older LGBTQIA+ adults in California
Authors: Tran, N. K.; Cicero, E.; Rosendale, N.; Sunder, G.; Dawson-Rose, C.; Flentje, A.
Abstract: Objectives: To examine which measure of socioeconomic position and socioenvironmental conditions has the strongest relationship with subjective cognitive decline (SCD) among midlife and older lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, intersex, asexual, and other sexual and gender minority (LGBTQIA+) adults. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional analysis of 3869 LGBTQIA+ adults aged 50 years or older participating in a community-engaged survey in California. Using logistic regression, we examined overall associations between each indicator of socioeconomic position and socioenvironmental conditions and SCD. We used a dominance analysis to assess the relative importance of each indicator based on the proportion of variance in SCD it explained. Results: Overall, 14.7% of the sample reported SCD. Midlife and older LGBTQIA+ adults in a lower socioeconomic position (i.e., lower education, unemployment, lower household income, fewer assets, financial insecurity, food insecurity, and unstable housing) had higher odds of SCD than those in a higher position, with significant odds ratios (OR) ranging from 1.44 to 1.93. In contrast, perceiving one's community as safe for LGBTQIA+ people was associated with lower odds of SCD (OR, 0.60; 95% CI, 0.48, 0.76). Dominance analysis indicated that household assets was the most important factor, explaining 2.8% of the variance in SCD (95% CI 2.2%, 3.6%), followed by household income (1.9%; 95% CI 1.2%, 2.7%) and perceived community safety (1.6%; 95% CI 1.1%, 2.3%). Discussion: Supporting the cognitive health of LGBTQIA+ people may require attention to both financial security across the life course and the broader social environments.

Title: Pneumococcal nasopharyngeal carriage in children 2-60 months of age in Novi Sad (Serbia), October 2022-September 2026
Authors: Petrovic, V. J.; Milosavljevic, B.; Djilas, M.; Markovic, M.; Vukovic, V.; Pustahija, T.; Rajcevic, S.; Medic, S.; Djekic-Malbasa, J.; Gvozdenac-Dragicevic, G.; Lazarevic, J.; Zelenovic, M.; Bjelic-Novakovic, R.; Trivic, S.; Kopcanski, S.; Andric, V.; Ristic, M.
Abstract: Background: Streptococcus pneumoniae nasopharyngeal carriage in young children is an important source of transmission and may precede pneumococcal disease. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccines can alter circulating serotypes. Continued surveillance is needed to monitor serotype replacement, vaccine serotype coverage, and antimicrobial resistance. Methods: A prospective surveillance study was conducted in outpatient pediatric practices from October 2022 to September 2026 among children aged 2-60 months in Novi Sad, Serbia. Healthy children attending preventive visits and children with acute respiratory tract infections were enrolled. Nasopharyngeal specimens were collected and cultured for S. pneumoniae. Participant-level analyses used the first eligible specimen per child, while isolate-level analyses included all recovered isolates. Serotyping and antimicrobial susceptibility testing were performed. Theoretical vaccine serotype coverage was estimated for licensed and selected investigational pneumococcal conjugate vaccines, with 23-valent polysaccharide vaccine evaluated separately. Results: Among 3,373 included children, 911 were pneumococcal carriers, giving an overall carriage prevalence of 27.0%. Carriage was higher among children with acute respiratory tract infection than among healthy children and was also associated with daycare attendance, chronic medical conditions, age, season, and surveillance year. In total, 1,312 pneumococcal isolates were recovered, of which 87.9% were typeable. The most frequent serotypes included 11A, 10A, 15A, 15B, 23A, 23B, 19A, and 6B. Theoretical serotype coverage was 8.2% for PCV10, 17.5% for PCV13, 20.0% for PCV15, and 47.3% for PCV20. More than half of typeable isolates were non-PCV20 serotypes. Resistance was most frequent to erythromycin, clindamycin, and tetracycline, while multidrug resistance was observed in 18.1% of isolates. Penicillin G non-susceptibility was uncommon. Conclusion: Pneumococcal carriage in children aged 2-60 months in Novi Sad was associated with age, clinical presentation, season, and surveillance year and involved diverse serotypes. Continued carriage surveillance, linked with invasive-disease and antibiotic-use data, would help determine whether the observed serotype and resistance patterns persist.

Title: Unboxing unhealthy food marketing: An analysis of the extent and nature of unhealthy food marketing to children on YouTube in Canada using the CHOPPED artificial intelligence system
Authors: Al Sharani, S.; Williamson, T.; Fietz, S.; Radin Pereira, L.; Elliott, C.; Potvin Kent, M.; Lalani, I.; Hossain, S.; Shakeri Hossein Abad, Z.; Yin, S.; Prowse, R.; Olstad, D. L.
Abstract: Background: Unhealthy food marketing negatively affects children's dietary patterns. However, little is known about the extent and nature of unhealthy food marketing to children on YouTube due to reliance on manual assessment methods. Objectives: To use a novel artificial intelligence (AI) system (CHild Oriented food Product Promotion Evaluation and Detection system, CHOPPED) to examine the extent and nature of unhealthy food marketing in YouTube videos suggested to Avatar accounts created for children and adults based on age and gender. Methods: Over two months of continuous monitoring, CHOPPED collected marketing instances played before, during, and after videos suggested by YouTube's algorithm to six child and two adult accounts that were not signed in and differed by age (2-4, 5-8, 9-12, =<18 years) and gender across four Canadian cities (Calgary, Vancouver, Toronto, Halifax). CHOPPED characterized the extent and nature of monthly child-targeted unhealthy food marketing instances during 24-hour and typical 2-hour daily viewing periods. Results: CHOPPED collected 60,633 marketing instances. No food marketing was shown to child accounts 2-4 years. On average, child accounts (5-12 years) were shown 25 monthly unhealthy food marketing instances during a 2-hour daily viewing period, 24 of which were child-targeted. The boy's account (9-12 years) was shown a significantly higher monthly frequency of child-targeted unhealthy food marketing instances (340, 70.2%) than the boy's account (5-8 years; 241, 66.2%), the girl's account (5-8 years; 261, 60.6%), the man's account (224, 57.7%), and the woman's account (263, 54.7%) during a 24-hour (p<0.05) but not a 2-hour daily viewing period. Monthly frequencies of some core child-targeted techniques shown to the boy's account (9-12 years) were also higher than other accounts during a 24-hour (p<0.05) but not a 2-hour daily viewing period. Conclusions: This study pioneered AI-driven analysis of the extent and nature of unhealthy food marketing to children on YouTube. Children's potential exposure to such marketing on YouTube may be low. There was some evidence that the older boys' account was shown more monthly child-targeted unhealthy food marketing instances and of some core child-targeted techniques than other accounts. On YouTube, food marketing may target a general audience rather than children by age and gender.

Title: Four waves of cancer-related risk behaviour and personal network data from a rural Romanian community
Authors: HANCEAN, M.-G.; GEANTA, M.; MOLINA, J. L.; LERNER, J.; GHITA, M.-C.; MIHAILA, B.-E.; VIDRASCU, B.-A.; CIOROBOIU, C.
Abstract: 4P-CAN is an EU-funded project that collected longitudinal personal network data to investigate how cancer-related risk behaviours are socially organised within a rural community. Respondents (egos) describe the people they know (alters), their relationships with them, and relationships among alters. We share four waves of data collected between September 2023 and September 2025 in a Romanian rural community through interviewer-assisted network interviews and link-tracing recruitment. Five linked data tables contain 353 interviews with 142 adults, 7,602 alter roster entries identifying 2,480 people, 41,354 records of ego-reported acquaintance between alters, and recruitment-node and referral records. Linking individuals across networks and waves supports investigation of how cancer-related risk behaviours are distributed and clustered across community relationships. It also supports research on network composition, overlapping networks, reported health attributes and longitudinal measurement. Reuse should account for non-probability recruitment, dependence among observations and changes in measurement across waves.

Title: Shifting source hubs and the factors associated with cross-country Zika virus transmission: a phylogeographic network analysis, 2012-2025
Authors: Pang, M.; Bu, X.; Liu, Q.; Li, C.; Chan, N.; Ji, H.; Qi, X.; Huang, Y.
Abstract: Background Zika virus local transmission has been reported in at least 97 countries and territories, but the sources, routes, and determinants of cross-country spread remain incompletely understood. We reconstructed a phylogeographic network, characterized source activity across epidemic phases, and examined factors associated with identified cross-country transmission events. Methodology/Principal Findings We analyzed a time-scaled Nextstrain phylogeny of 1,043 Zika virus genomes collected between February 2013 and March 2026. Parent-child branches assigned to different locations were screened and consolidated into 81 source-destination-year events involving 39 locations. Network analysis characterized temporal and geographic patterns, routes, hubs, and communities. For the analysis of associated factors, 68 events with complete covariate data were compared, using mixed-effects models, with eligible year-matched control records for which no event was identified, with all 68 events retained and a new control set drawn in each of 200 iterations. Asia contributed the earliest event, from Thailand in 2012. Most events occurred within the Americas (79.0%) and were concentrated during 2014-2016, with Brazil as the principal source hub. All six events from 2019 onward originated from Thailand or India and reached destinations in Asia, Europe, and Africa. Thailand's source activity spanned 2012-2025. Event identification was positively associated with high source-country incidence (odds ratio [OR], 2.66; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.39-9.69), greater air travel (OR, 2.52; 95% CI, 1.58-5.67), and higher destination-country GNI per capita (OR, 1.70; 95% CI, 1.20-4.50). It was negatively associated with greater geographic distance (OR, 0.11; 95% CI, 0.02-0.20) and higher source-country GNI per capita (OR, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.45-0.94). Fourteen source countries showed elevated residual source propensities, with Brazil and Thailand among the highest. Conclusions/Significance The transmission network showed a shift in dominant source hubs, from early activity in Asia to the Americas during the 2014-2016 epidemic and back to Asia in recent years. High source-country incidence, greater air travel, and shorter distance can help identify country pairs requiring closer surveillance, alongside established routes in the Americas and persistent or emerging Asian sources, particularly as El Nino may increase vector-borne transmission potential in 2026-2027.

Title: Investigating Differential Changes in Cardiovascular Mortality by Documented diabetes in the United States Before and During the COVID-19 Pandemic: A Comparative Time-Series Analysis
Authors: Ghani, M. U.; Chang, H.; Shuhag, S.; Kamath, S.; Chughtai, S.; Bhuiyan, M. A. N.; Rodriguez, C. J.
Abstract: Background: Whether diabetes modified pandemic-related changes in cardiovascular disease (CVD) mortality remains uncertain. We examined differential changes in US CVD mortality among deaths with versus without diabetes documented on the death certificate. Methods: We analyzed CDC WONDER Multiple Cause of Death data from 2005 to 2024, identifying deaths with CVD as the underlying cause among adults aged 25 years. Cohorts were CVD deaths with diabetes documented as a contributing cause (CVD+DM) and CVD deaths without documented diabetes. Because pre-2020 trajectories differed, the primary comparison of age-adjusted rates used a comparative interrupted time-series model allowing cohort-specific pre-2020 trends. Difference-in-differences estimates (2015-2019 vs 2020-2024) were descriptive. Results: CVD+DM mortality declined from 43.1 per 100,000 in 2005 to 34.3 in 2019 and was 38.4 in 2024; mortality without documented diabetes declined from 398.7 to 296.6 and was 289.8. In the primary analysis, CVD+DM mortality showed a 13.1% greater relative level increase at 2020 (95% CI, 10.4%-15.9%), with no significant differential change in slope thereafter. Descriptively, the ratio of rate ratios was 1.16, and the absolute difference-in-differences was 5.0 per 100,000. Conclusions: After accounting for cohort-specific pre-2020 trends, CVD mortality with documented diabetes showed a greater relative increase at the 2020 transition. These findings describe differential mortality patterns rather than a causal effect of diabetes or the pandemic. Keywords: Cardiovascular mortality; Diabetes; COVID-19; Difference-in-differences; Preventive Cardiology Nonstandard Abbreviations and Acronyms AAMR: age-adjusted mortality rate APC: annual percentage change CITS: comparative interrupted time-series CVD+DM: cardiovascular disease deaths with diabetes documented as contributing cause DID: differences-in-differences DM: diabetes mellitus

Title: Projected prevalence and number of persons with diagnosed type 2 diabetes by socioeconomic position in Germany between 2022 and 2060
Authors: Piedboeuf-Potyka, K.; Hering, R.; Schulz, M.; Mackowiak, M.; Brinks, R.; Hoyer, A.; Wirth, M.; Toennies, T.
Abstract: Background: Current projections of the prevalence and number of persons with type 2 diabetes by socioeconomic position (SEP) are lacking for Germany. This study aims to project age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence in Germany by sex and SEP between 2022 and 2060. Methods: We used a partial differential equation (PDE) based on the illness-death model to project age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence by sex and SEP between 2022 and 2060. The PDE describes the relationship between prevalence, incidence, all-cause mortality and the mortality rate ratio (MRR) of individuals with vs. without type2 diabetes considering age, calendar year and SEP. SEP was measured by quintiles of the German Index of Socioeconomic Deprivation (GISD). Baseline prevalence, incidence, and MRR in 2022 were derived from statutory health insurance data (~85% of the German population). Projected prevalence was multiplied by population projections from the German Federal Statistical Office to estimate the number of persons with diabetes. Results: Type 2 diabetes prevalence increases with age, peaking between 80 and 90 years. Between 2022 and 2060, age-specific prevalence is projected to increase for both sexes across all SEP groups. SEP-related disparities persisted with largest differences between the highest (5th GISD quintile) and lowest (1st GISD quintile) SEP group. The number of persons with type 2 diabetes is projected to rise from 8.4 million in 2022 to between 11.2 and 19.2 million in 2060. Conclusions: Between 2022 and 2060, age-specific type 2 diabetes prevalence is projected to increase with increasing socioeconomic inequalities.
